meta.title: Who really said "One of the oldest human needs is having someone to wonder where you are when you don't come home at night"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Widely credited to Margaret Mead, but with no primary source: the earliest citation is a 1991 anthology, published after her 1978 death.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'One of the oldest human needs is having someone to wonder where you are when you don't come home at night'?
meta.ogDescription: No primary source ties this line to Margaret Mead. Print appearances begin in 1982; the citation of record is a 1991 anthology.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The line is credited to Mead everywhere it appears, and the thought sits comfortably beside her lifelong writing on family and belonging — but no book, column, lecture or interview of hers has ever been produced for it. The oldest citation anyone offers is an anthology published in 1991, after her death in 1978, and the earliest printings we could locate date from 1982.

source.heading: Where the trail actually starts
source.excerpt: One of the oldest human needs is having someone to wonder where you are when you don’t come home at night.
trail: Wikiquote’s Margaret Mead page ↗ carries the line with exactly one citation: “Attributed in The Quotable Woman (1991) by the Running Press, p. 53.” That is an anthology published after Mead’s death in 1978 — a record of the attribution, not of anything she wrote.

WIST Quotations ↗ files the saying under Attributed, cites no primary source, and notes the variant form “Having someone wonder where you are when you don’t come home at night is a very old human need.”

AZQuotes ↗ reprints the line among its top Mead quotations with no citation at all, and Goodreads ↗ carries the variant wording with no book or date, under its own notice that quotes are community-added and unverified.

Mead is a magnet for sourceless lines. Quote Investigator’s study of the “healed femur” story traced its propagation ↗ to Paul Brand’s 1980 and 1993 books and observed that in a 1968 interview Mead defined civilization quite differently. Quote Investigator has no article on the ‘come home at night’ line at all.
source.excerptNote: A second wording circulates just as widely and is recorded by WIST as a variant of the same saying: “Having someone wonder where you are when you don’t come home at night is a very old human need.” Neither form comes attached to a work, a date or a page.
source.rightsNote: Because no work has been identified as the origin of this sentence, no copyright status can honestly be asserted. If it does turn out to be Mead’s, it would date from her working life and would be in copyright, controlled by her estate and the original publisher; if it is an anonymous paraphrase, its status is simply unknown. Either way it is not safe to treat as public domain.

author.name: Margaret Mead
author.heading: Who was Margaret Mead?
author.metaLine: 1901–1978 · American cultural anthropologist and public intellectual
author.bio: Margaret Mead (16 December 1901 – 15 November 1978) was the best-known anthropologist of her century and, for much of it, the discipline’s public face in America. She was curator of ethnology at the American Museum of Natural History and president of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, and wrote Coming of Age in Samoa (1928), Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935) and the memoir Blackberry Winter (1972). Her fame is also her quotation problem: an authoritative-sounding name attached to a warm observation about human nature is rarely challenged, and several of the lines most often printed under her name have no located source.

misattribution.heading: Why the attribution is shakier than it looks
misattribution.intro: Nobody claims a different author for this line, and that is precisely what lets it travel unchallenged. The problem is not a rival name — it is that the citation chain has no bottom.

items.who: BrainyQuote, AZQuotes, Goodreads and their imitators
items.why: These sites print the sentence under Mead’s name with no work, page or date. AZQuotes ↗ gives sources for some Mead entries but none for this one, and Goodreads ↗ flags its own quotations as community-submitted and unverified.

This anthology is the single source Wikiquote ↗ can point to, and it was published in 1991 — Mead died in 1978. An anthology attributing a line is evidence that the attribution existed by 1991, not evidence that Mead said it.

WIST ↗ records the saying in two shapes — the “One of the oldest human needs…” version and “Having someone wonder where you are… is a very old human need.” Genuine quotations from a printed source tend to stabilise; free-floating ones drift, because there is no page to check them against.

items.who: Margaret Mead as a quotation magnet
items.why: Her most-shared lines are repeatedly the least documented. Quote Investigator found that the famous “healed femur” anecdote rests on one man’s recollection ↗ rather than on anything Mead published.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest position: this is a saying attributed to Margaret Mead, not a documented one. Until someone produces a column, book, lecture or interview, the earliest thing anyone can actually cite is a 1991 anthology ↗ published after her death.

context.heading: Why it sounds so much like her
lead: Mead spent fifty years arguing that the things people treat as private feelings are in fact social arrangements — that kinship, marriage and household are inventions a culture keeps rebuilding. A sentence that reframes love as an old human need for someone to notice your absence is exactly the move she made for a living, which is a large part of why the attribution has never been questioned.

She also had the platform for it. Alongside the scholarship she wrote a monthly column in Redbook with Rhoda Métraux, according to her Wikipedia biography ↗, and spoke constantly on radio and television. Thousands of pages of accessible, aphoristic Mead exist — which makes it all the more striking that nobody has ever pointed to the page this one is on.
detailsBody: A phrase search of the Newspapers.com archive (subscription required) returns no printing of either wording before 1982; the earliest hits are the Port Huron, Michigan Times Herald of 29 July 1982 and a slightly earlier June 1982 appearance of the shortened phrase. Mead died on 15 November 1978. That gap does not prove she never said it — a line can sit in a magazine column for years before a columnist picks it up — but a saying this quotable usually leaves fingerprints while its author is still alive to be quoted.

Two research resources that would ordinarily settle this both fall silent. Quote Investigator ↗ has taken on other Mead attributions but has never published on this one, and WIST ↗, which cites primary sources wherever it can, marks this entry simply “Attributed.” When the careful compilers decline to source a line, that absence is itself the finding.
context.pull: An anthology attributing a line proves the attribution existed. It does not prove the author did.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Margaret Mead page contains this quote and its only citation is "Attributed in The Quotable Woman (1991) by the Running Press, p. 53"; the page's top-level sections are Quotes, Quotes about Margaret Mead, Disputed, and External links.

WIST Quotations lists the quote under Margaret Mead with status "Attributed," no primary source cited, and records the variant "Having someone wonder where you are when you don't come home at night is a very old human need."

Quote Investigator's article on the "healed femur" quote concludes that Paul Brand was the key propagator of the anecdote via his 1980 and 1993 books, and notes a 1968 interview in which Mead defined civilization differently.

Wikipedia gives Margaret Mead's dates as 16 December 1901 – 15 November 1978, her role as curator of ethnology at the American Museum of Natural History, her monthly Redbook column co-authored with Rhoda Métraux, and her books Coming of Age in Samoa (1928), Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935) and Blackberry Winter (1972).

Goodreads carries the variant wording "Having someone wonder where you are when you don't come home at night is a very old human need," credited to Margaret Mead with no source, alongside a notice that quotes are added by the community and not verified by Goodreads.

AZQuotes lists "One of the oldest human needs is having someone to wonder where you are when you don't come home at night" among its featured Margaret Mead quotations with no source citation, though other quotes on the page do carry citations.
Lib Quotes gives the citation for this quote as "Attributed in The Quotable Woman (1991) by the Running Press, p. 53."
A Quote Investigator site search for the phrase "come home at night" returns no results, confirming QI has not investigated this quote.
